title: 409A Safe Harbor Explained: The Three Paths and Why They Matter
summary: The 409A safe harbor under Treasury Reg 1.409A-1 gives a rebuttable presumption of reasonableness. Here are the three paths, when each fits, and what voids it.
body_markdown:
## What Is a 409A Valuation?


The 409A safe harbor is the rebuttable presumption of reasonableness in Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2), and it shifts the burden of proof to the IRS. A 409A valuation is the independent appraisal of a private company’s common stock fair market value that can earn that presumption, and once it does, the government can only defeat your number by proving it was grossly unreasonable. Indinero delivers that appraisal as a written report inside a CFO advisory engagement, so the number that defends your strike price is the same one that hits your books.


Most founders meet this rule in the wrong order. They grant options first, price them off a figure someone sketched in a board deck, and learn what Section 409A is during diligence two years later.


That’s the expensive order of operations.


Congress added Section 409A to the tax code in section 885 of the[American Jobs Creation Act of 2004](https://www.congress.gov/108/plaws/publ357/PLAW-108publ357.pdf) , signed October 22, 2004. Treasury and the IRS wrote the governing rules in T.D. 9321, published at[72 FR 19234 on April 17, 2007](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2007-04-17/pdf/07-1820.pdf) , effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2008. You can read the[Treasury announcement on the guidance](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/js2162) and the statute itself at[26 U.S. Code Section 409A](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/409A) .


Here’s the trap. Section 409A governs nonqualified deferred compensation, and[IRS Notice 2005-1](https://www.irs.gov/irb/2005-02_IRB) established that an option granted with an exercise price below the fair market value of the stock on the grant date provides for a deferral of compensation. Grant options cheap, skip a defensible valuation, and the IRS can tax the holder on paper gains they never cashed out.


A 409A answers one question with a number. What is a share of common stock worth today, on an arm’s length basis, given everything known about the business.


A valuation that actually qualifies has five parts:


- **A written report.** Not a spreadsheet tab and not a board resolution. The regulation asks for a report that walks through the required factors.
- **A valuator the company reasonably determines is qualified.** The standard differs by which safe harbor path you take, and the difference matters more than most content admits.
- **A 12-month shelf life at the outside.** Under Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(i) the appraisal must be dated no more than 12 months before the transaction it supports.
- **One of three safe harbor paths.** Independent appraisal, formula price, or the illiquid start-up route.
- **A downstream accounting use.** The same fair value becomes the current price input under ASC 718.


That’s a different question than a funding round answers. A priced round values preferred stock. A 409A values common stock for option grants. For more context on the equity itself, see our[guide to common stock for business owners](https://www.indinero.com/blog/a-business-owners-guide-to-common-stock/) , and for the full picture,[the essential guide to 409A valuations](https://www.indinero.com/resources/the-essential-guide-for-409a-valuations/) .


## Who Needs a 409A


Any private company that issues stock options or other equity compensation needs a 409A valuation. The requirement flows from IRC Section 409A, and it is not limited to venture-backed Delaware C-corporations.


It reaches further than most founders assume. Bootstrapped companies granting a first option pool. PE-backed companies. LLCs that grant profits interests or option-equivalent units. S-corporations with equity incentive plans. Multi-entity groups that push equity down to operating subsidiaries.


The trigger is issuing equity compensation, not raising venture capital. A profitable, self-funded SaaS company that grants its first option needs a 409A before that grant. A company preparing a priced round needs a fresh one, because the new preferred price is material information about value. A company that hasn’t granted in 18 months and is about to reload the pool needs a current appraisal, because the old one has gone stale.


The common triggers, in the order companies usually hit them:


- **The first option grant.** Before the grant, not after the offer letter goes out.
- **A closed priced round.** The new preferred price is exactly the kind of recent arm’s length transaction the regulation tells an appraiser to weigh.
- **A secondary sale or tender offer.** Employee liquidity at a price above the common value is now routine, and it feeds straight back into the next report.
- **M&A conversations or a signed LOI.** A term sheet changes the picture before it changes the cap table.
- **IPO preparation.** Auditors and underwriters read every report in the chain.


Here is the part that surprises people. If the valuation fails, the tax liability belongs to the option holder, usually your employee, not to the company. The reporting obligation, though, is yours. Per the[IRS General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/iw2w3) , Box 12 Code Y reports deferrals under a Section 409A plan, and Box 12 Code Z reports income under a nonqualified deferred compensation plan that fails to satisfy Section 409A. The Code Z amount also lands in Box 1. For nonemployees, the[Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099mec) put Section 409A deferrals of at least $2,000 in Form 1099-MISC Box 12 and amounts includible in income under Section 409A in Box 15.


So the company that gets the valuation wrong hands its own team a tax bill and then files the paperwork that documents it. That is the employee-relations problem, the diligence finding, and the indemnity negotiation, all from one missing report.


Two roles usually own the decision. Founders getting their first valuation ahead of a round or a grant, and Controllers who manage the ongoing refresh cadence alongside stock-compensation accounting. If your team is weighing early exercise and[83(b) election timing](https://www.indinero.com/blog/83b-startup-taxes/) , the 409A number feeds that analysis too. Our short answer on[who can perform a 409A valuation](https://www.indinero.com/faq/who-can-perform-a-409a-valuation/) covers the qualification question on its own.


## The Safe Harbor Framework


The 409A safe harbor lives in Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2), titled “Presumption of reasonableness.” That precision matters. Subparagraph (B)(1) is the general reasonableness rule that applies to everyone, and it is not the safe harbor. The safe harbor is (B)(2), and the three qualifying methods are (B)(2)(i), (B)(2)(ii) and (B)(2)(iii). The text is published at the[Cornell Legal Information Institute](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.409A-1) and the[Electronic Code of Federal Regulations](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/section-1.409A-1) .


The operative sentence reads:


> “For purposes of this paragraph (b)(5)(iv)(B), the use of any of the following methods of valuation is presumed to result in a reasonable valuation, provided that the Commissioner may rebut such a presumption upon a showing that either the valuation method or the application of such method was grossly unreasonable.”
>
>
> Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)


Here’s why that presumption matters. In an ordinary tax dispute, the taxpayer defends its position. Under the safe harbor, that flips. The IRS carries the burden, and it can overturn a qualifying valuation only by clearing the grossly-unreasonable bar. The regulation never defines the phrase, which is itself worth knowing. It is plainly a higher standard than “wrong” or “aggressive.”


So the 409A rebuttable presumption is not a shield. The agency can still challenge your number. It just has to show gross unreasonableness rather than simple disagreement. That’s the difference between defending a well-supported appraisal and defending a napkin.


One more subparagraph almost nobody covers. Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(3), “Use of alternative methods,” confirms a company may use different valuation methods for different actions. You are not locked into one method forever across every grant, repurchase and transfer. And the law on top of all this has been stable for nearly two decades. The June 2016 proposed regulations, REG-123854-12, published in[Internal Revenue Bulletin 2016-28](https://www.irs.gov/irb/2016-28_IRB) , are still only proposed, and they do not rewrite section 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv).


### The Three Safe Harbor Paths


Treasury Reg 1.409A-1 lists exactly three methods that earn the presumption. Most companies use the first. The other two exist for narrower situations.


**1. The independent appraisal method, Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(i).** The regulation describes it in one sentence:


> “A valuation of a class of stock determined by an independent appraisal that meets the requirements of section 401(a)(28)(C) and the regulations as of a date that is no more than 12 months before the relevant transaction to which the valuation is applied (for example, the date of grant of a stock option).”
>
>
> Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(i)


A 409A independent appraisal is the path nearly every growth-stage and VC-backed company uses, and it’s the version that holds up in a data room. Note what it does not contain. No company-age limit, no 90-day change-of-control test, no 180-day offering test. Those gates belong to path three. What it does carry is the 12-month dating rule and, underneath it, the (B)(1) material-information rule. An appraisal that is four months old but predates a signed term sheet or a lost anchor customer is exposed regardless of the calendar. Our rundown of[the essentials of 409A valuations](https://www.indinero.com/blog/irs-409a/) walks through what a defensible report includes.


**2. The formula price method, Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(ii).** A company sets value by formula, for example a fixed multiple of revenue or book value, as long as that formula would be treated as fair market value under Treasury Reg 1.83-5 when used as a nonlapse restriction under[Treasury Reg 1.83-3(h)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.83-3) . Most articles wave at this path and call it rare. The specific reasons it’s rare are four operating constraints that never expire:


- **Universal consistency.** The stock has to be valued the same way for any transfer to the issuer or to any holder of more than 10 percent of total combined voting power. The attribution rules of section 1.424-1(d) apply, so family and entity holdings aggregate in that 10 percent test. A founder buyback, a departing-employee repurchase and an insider secondary all price off the same formula.
- **One narrow escape hatch.** The consistency requirement carves out an arm’s length transaction involving the sale of all or substantially all of the outstanding stock. A whole-company sale prices freely. Nothing smaller does.
- **A hard exclusion for transferable option stock.** The subparagraph does not apply where stock acquired on exercise is transferable other than through a nonlapse restriction. That alone disqualifies most conventional startup option plans.
- **The restriction can never lapse.** Section 1.83-3(h) requires a permanent limitation on transferability. A restriction that falls away at IPO or on a change of control is a lapse restriction and does not qualify.


Read together, path two is built for a company that intends to stay closely held permanently. A venture-backed SaaS company raising priced rounds and planning an exit is structurally incompatible with it.


**3. The illiquid start-up method, Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(iii).** This is the written report from a qualified person, and it has four gates:


1. **Age and liquidity.** The company must have no material trade or business that it or any predecessor conducted for 10 years or more, and no class of equity traded on an established securities market. The predecessor language matters. A recapitalization or reincorporation does not restart the clock.
2. **No anticipated liquidity event.** The path is unavailable if a change in control is reasonably anticipated within 90 days of the action, or a public offering within 180 days.
3. **No put or call.** The stock cannot be subject to a put, call or similar purchase right, with carve-outs for a right of first refusal on a third-party offer and for a right that is itself a lapse restriction.
4. **A qualified person and a written report.** The valuation must be made reasonably and in good faith, evidenced by a written report, and it must address the (B)(1) factors.


### Who Counts as a Qualified Appraiser


The regulation answers this twice, with two different standards, and collapsing them is the most common error in 409A content.


For path three, the regulation supplies its own test:


> “a valuation will not be treated as made reasonably and in good faith unless the valuation is performed by a person or persons that the corporation reasonably determines is qualified to perform such a valuation based on the person’s or persons’ significant knowledge, experience, education, or training.”
>
>
> Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(iii)


And it quantifies the experience piece:


> “For this purpose, significant experience generally means at least five years of relevant experience in business valuation or appraisal, financial accounting, investment banking, private equity, secured lending, or other comparable experience in the line of business or industry in which the service recipient operates.”
>
>
> Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(iii)


That five-year language belongs to path three. It is not the path one standard, even though it gets quoted as if it were.


Path one runs through a chain of cross-references instead. Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(i) requires an appraisal meeting[IRC section 401(a)(28)(C)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/401) , the ESOP valuation rule, which in turn requires an appraiser meeting requirements similar to the regulations under section 170(a)(1). Those regulations are today[Treasury Reg 1.170A-17](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.170A-17) , the qualified appraiser rules finalized in 2018. Under 1.170A-17(b)(2), an appraiser qualifies either by completing professional or college-level coursework in valuing that type of property plus two or more years of experience valuing it, or by holding a recognized appraiser designation awarded on the basis of demonstrated competency.


Three designations fill that gap in practice, and they are not interchangeable:


- **ASA, Accredited Senior Appraiser.** Issued by the[American Society of Appraisers](https://www.appraisers.org/) . The business valuation track requires five years of full-time business valuation experience, 108 classroom hours across four examined courses, two peer-reviewed appraisal submissions, and a USPAP exam. It maps onto both the recognized-designation route for path one and the five-year language in path three.
- **ABV, Accredited in Business Valuation.** Issued by the AICPA and the only one of the three that requires a current CPA license. ABV holders follow the AICPA Statement on Standards for Valuation Services.
- **CVA, Certified Valuation Analyst.** Issued by[NACVA](https://www.nacva.com/cvaqualifications) . Requires a degree or equivalent plus the combined equivalent of two years of full-time valuation experience, training and a comprehensive exam. It satisfies the coursework-plus-two-years route in 1.170A-17(b)(2) and is the most common credential in the mid-market.


One myth worth retiring. “Internal valuations never qualify for safe harbor” is an accurate description of path one and an inaccurate description of path three, whose test is written around the corporation’s own reasonable determination and the reliance of a reasonable individual. The five-year list expressly includes financial accounting, investment banking and private equity experience, not appraisal alone.


### What Voids the Safe Harbor Presumption


The presumption falls away the moment the valuation stops being reasonable under the regulation’s own conditions.


- **The 12-month wall.** Under (B)(1), a previously calculated value is unreasonable once it was calculated with respect to a date more than 12 months earlier than the date it’s being used for. Grants signed on day 366 sit outside the harbor even if nothing in the business changed.
- **New material information.** Also under (B)(1), a value fails if the calculation doesn’t reflect information available after the calculation date that may materially affect value. This runs independently of the 12-month clock.
- **Omission of a required factor.** The regulation names tangible and intangible assets, the present value of anticipated future cash flows, the market value of comparable companies, recent arm’s length transactions in the stock, control premiums and discounts for lack of marketability. A report that never addresses comparables or a recent secondary is exposed on its face.
- **Falling out of a path three gate.** Crossing ten years of operating history, signing a term sheet that makes a change in control reasonably anticipated within 90 days, moving toward an offering inside 180 days, or adding a put or call.
- **Breaking consistency under path two.** A single off-formula insider repurchase compromises the used-consistently condition.
- **Material misstatement or omission to the appraiser.** An incomplete cap table, an unmentioned LOI, a withheld secondary. That attacks the application prong, which is one of the two things the Commissioner is allowed to attack.


Stale 409As fail. Miss any of those conditions and the number might still be right, but you lose the burden-shifting benefit and have to defend the valuation on its own merits.


### What Happens When the Presumption Is Rebutted


If the IRS clears the grossly-unreasonable bar, the option is treated as discounted, which makes it deferred compensation inside Section 409A. The consequences stack in a specific order.


**Income inclusion, at vesting.** Under IRC section 409A(a)(1)(A), the deferred compensation is includible in gross income to the extent it isn’t subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture. For a discounted option, that risk lapses at vesting. Income is recognized tranche by tranche as the option vests, not at exercise and not at sale. An option holder who never exercised anything can owe tax.


**A 20 percent additional tax.** IRC section 409A(a)(1)(B)(i)(II) imposes an amount equal to 20 percent of the compensation required to be included in income. That sits on top of ordinary income tax and applicable payroll tax.


**Premium interest.** Section 409A(a)(1)(B)(i)(I) adds interest at the underpayment rate plus one percentage point, applied to the underpayments that would have occurred had the income been recognized in the year first deferred. The IRS held rates steady for the quarter beginning October 1, 2026, with the individual underpayment rate at 7 percent compounded daily ([IRS, fourth quarter 2026 interest rates](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/interest-rates-remain-the-same-for-the-fourth-quarter-of-2026) ). That puts the Section 409A premium rate at 8 percent compounded daily for that quarter.


**A second layer in California.** California conforms to Section 409A through Revenue and Taxation Code section 17501. AB 1173 added R&TC section 17508.2, substituting 5 percent for 20 percent as the California additional tax, effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2013 ([Cooley on the change](https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2013/california-reduces-section-409a-state-income-tax-penalty) ). For a Bay Area company the combined additional tax is 25 percent, plus premium interest at both levels.


**Case law exists, and there’s only one that counts.** In *Sutardja v. United States* , decided by the U.S. Court of Federal Claims on February 27, 2013, the court held that Section 409A applies to discounted stock options and rejected the argument that no taxable event occurs until exercise, then remanded on whether the option was in fact granted at a discount. It remains the principal judicial authority on the question ([Morgan Lewis analysis](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2013/03/eb_lf_courtaffirmssection409aappliestodiscountedstockoptions_21mar13) ).


The safe harbor is what keeps that entire sequence from ever starting.


## The Valuation Methodology


A defensible 409A is a two-stage exercise. Stage one establishes total equity value. Stage two allocates that value across the capital structure to reach a common stock price. Both stages have to satisfy the standard in Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(1):


> “the fair market value of the stock as of a valuation date means a value determined by the reasonable application of a reasonable valuation method”
>
>
> Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(1)


Stage one runs on three accepted approaches, plus a fourth route that shows up constantly in venture-backed companies.


Approach What it does Where it fits


Income Discounts projected free cash flows at a risk-adjusted rate and adds a terminal value Strong for a SaaS business with contracted ARR and observable retention. Weak pre-revenue.


Market Prices the company against guideline public companies and guideline transactions, usually on EV/ARR or EV/revenue for software Comparable-set selection is the most contested judgment in the report, and the place a grossly-unreasonable-application argument would start.


Asset Works from adjusted net asset value Holding companies, asset-heavy balance sheets, wind-downs. Rarely the primary approach for software.


Backsolve Solves for total equity value implied by the price paid in a recent priced round The default when a priced round closed recently.


Allocation is where the common stock number actually gets set. The reference here is the AICPA’s[Accounting and Valuation Guide for privately held company equity securities issued as compensation](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/cpe-learning/publication/valuation-of-privately-held-company-equity-securities-issued-as-compensation-accounting-and-valuation-guide-OPL) , the book appraisers and auditors call the cheap stock guide.


Allocation method How it works When it fits


CVM, current value method Runs the liquidation waterfall on today’s equity value and today’s capital structure A liquidity event is imminent, or the company has made no material progress against plan. Not forward looking.


OPM, option pricing method Treats each class as a call option on total equity value, with strikes set by liquidation preferences and conversion points The default for a company three to five years from liquidity. Sensitive to volatility and expected time to exit.


PWERM Models discrete exit scenarios, weights them by probability, discounts each at a risk-adjusted rate Exit timing is short, usually under 12 months, and outcomes are predictable. Not suited to option-like payoffs.


Hybrid PWERM scenarios with OPM allocation inside each branch Several plausible near-term outcomes, with option-like payoff behavior still mattering inside each one.


For most growth-stage SaaS companies, that means OPM with a backsolve to the most recent priced round, moving to a hybrid once an exit path narrows. A discount for lack of marketability is then applied to the allocated common value, and DLOM magnitude is the second most contested judgment in the report after the comparable set. It isn’t an aggressive add-on. The regulation’s own factor list names control premiums and discounts for lack of marketability directly.


Two currency notes. The methodology framework traces back to[Revenue Ruling 59-60](https://www.taxnotes.com/research/federal/irs-guidance/revenue-rulings/rev-rul-59-60/d30t) , whose eight factors for valuing closely held stock map almost one to one onto the 409A factor list. And the AICPA is revising the guide right now. On December 21, 2025 its Financial Reporting Executive Committee released a[working draft updating Chapters 6 and 8](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/advocacy/download/working-draft-of-the-updated-valuation-of-privately-held-company-equity-unpublished) , with comments due June 1, 2026, adding guidance on testing the implied credit spread in complex capital structures and on identifying the principal market when inferring value from secondary transactions. The law on top has been stable. The practice underneath it is moving.


The output is a single per-share common fair market value. That figure becomes the option strike price and the input to stock-compensation accounting. Indinero produces that analysis as part of its[409A valuation services](https://www.indinero.com/services/409a-valuation-services/) .


## What Drives 409A Cost


Three things move the price of a 409A engagement: company stage, capital-structure complexity, and turnaround speed. All three trace back to how much analysis a defensible number under IRC Section 409A actually requires.


An early, pre-revenue company with a single common class and one seed round is cheap to value, because the analysis is thin. A later-stage company is not. Several preferred rounds, participating preferences, warrants, SAFEs still on the books, secondary transactions, and international entities all add hours. An OPM-to-PWERM hybrid, convertible instruments, and multi-entity structures push the work up further. Rush timelines cost more. So does the documentation depth an auditor will demand at year end.

One buying note the price tags hide. A provider advertising analysts with five or more years of experience is quoting the qualification language from path three, Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(iii). Ask which safe harbor your provider is actually delivering into, because one of those paths closes at ten years of operating history and the other doesn’t.


Here’s the part founders get backward. The cheapest 409A is not the goal. The defensible one is. A lowball appraisal that omits a recent secondary sale or ignores a signed term sheet is the exact omission of material information that voids the safe harbor. Price is a poor proxy for defensibility.

## When to Refresh


Refresh a 409A on a 12-month clock or on a material event, whichever comes first. The rule runs from both directions. Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(1) makes a value calculated more than 12 months before the date of use unreasonable, and (B)(2)(i) requires the independent appraisal to be dated no more than 12 months before the transaction it supports.


Material events reset the clock before the year is up:


1. A priced equity round closing, including a bridge that converts or carries a cap that reprices the company.
2. A secondary transaction or tender offer in your own shares.
3. A signed term sheet or letter of intent for an acquisition.
4. A significant acquisition or divestiture.
5. A material change in the financial plan in either direction, including an anchor customer lost or won.
6. A recapitalization, a new preferred series with different preferences, or an option pool change that alters the waterfall.
7. Any concrete move toward or away from an IPO, or crossing a path three gate such as ten years of operating history.


Secondaries deserve their own line. A tender offer priced above the common value is precisely the recent arm’s length transaction the regulation’s factor list tells an appraiser to weigh, and the AICPA’s December 2025 working draft sharpens how those prices feed the common share price. A 409A page written in 2026 that treats secondaries as a footnote is behind the practice.


Refresh before, not after. The most common failure is granting on an out-of-date figure in the window between a material event and the next appraisal.


If a discounted option has already been granted, there’s a narrow fix. IRS Notice 2008-113 permits an upward repricing of the exercise price to the grant-date fair market value, and[Notice 2010-6](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-10-06.pdf) clarifies it. Three conditions decide whether you’re inside the window, as summarized in the *Journal of Accountancy* ‘s[review of upward stock option repricing](https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2011/sep/20114296/) . The price must have been set below fair market value in error. The repricing must happen before the holder exercises, and an already-exercised option cannot be corrected even in the same tax year. For a section 16 insider the deadline is the last day of the tax year of grant, and for everyone else the last day of the following tax year.


Read those deadlines against a real timeline. A company that discovers a valuation problem during Series B diligence, two years after the grants, is usually outside the window entirely. The cheapest compliance spend is a refresh before the grant, not a cleanup after.


A company that grants regularly usually runs a standing quarterly review, so a material event never catches it mid-grant on a stale number. That cadence is easier to hold when the 409A sits with the team that already tracks your numbers. The events that void a valuation, a converting bridge, a signed LOI, a secondary, a reset forecast, all surface in the monthly close and the board package before anyone thinks to order an appraisal. With indinero, refresh timing is coordinated with your funding calendar as part of a year-round finance partnership, not a transactional appraisal you have to remember to reorder. The[409A engagement timeline](https://www.indinero.com/blog/409a-engagement-timeline/) shows how that sequencing works, and our short answer covers[how long a 409A valuation is good for](https://www.indinero.com/faq/how-long-is-a-409a-valuation-good-for/) .


## The 409A and ASC 718 Connection


The 409A fair market value does double duty. It sets the tax-side strike price, and it feeds the accounting-side expense under ASC 718.


FASB Accounting Standards Codification Topic 718, Compensation, Stock Compensation, requires companies to measure equity awards at grant-date fair value and expense that amount over the service period, generally the vesting schedule. Grant-date fair value comes out of an option-pricing model, usually Black-Scholes or a lattice model, whose inputs are the current price of the underlying share, the exercise price, expected term, expected volatility, the risk-free rate and expected dividends. The 409A supplies the current price, and usually the strike as well.


Does a 409A satisfy ASC 718? Under one specific expedient, yes. FASB issued[ASU 2021-07](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU_2021-07.pdf) on October 25, 2021, giving nonpublic entities a practical expedient to determine the current price input using the reasonable application of a reasonable valuation method, and it names a valuation performed under the Section 409A regulations as an example of one. One valuation can serve both the tax rule and Topic 718. The guardrails travel with it. The value can’t be calculated more than 12 months before the measurement date, it has to be updated for later information material to the entity’s value, and the expedient is applied measurement date by measurement date to all equity-classified awards on the same underlying share.


So a weak or stale 409A doesn’t just create tax exposure. It corrupts the stock-compensation expense that flows through the income statement and into your audited financials. One bad number, two broken workstreams.


The downstream effects are specific:


- **P&L and EBITDA.** Stock compensation expense is a non-cash charge against GAAP operating income and the most common line in an adjusted EBITDA bridge, which boards and lenders read closely.
- **Board and investor reporting.** A refreshed 409A that moves the common price moves the expense run rate, which moves the forecast. Controllers who hear about a refresh after the fact get a restated expense schedule.
- **Audit readiness.** For a first audit, the 409A report is a workpaper. Auditors test the valuator’s competence, the comparable set, the volatility assumption and the DLOM.
- **R&D credit interaction.** Qualified research expenses under IRC section 41 are built largely on W-2 Box 1 wages. A Section 409A failure pushes Code Z income into Box 1, which changes the wage base a QRE calculation starts from.

## Frequently asked questions


Common questions about the 409A safe harbor, the three qualifying paths, and what happens when the presumption is challenged.


### What is the 409A safe harbor in plain English?


The 409A safe harbor is a rebuttable presumption that your common stock valuation is reasonable, which shifts the burden of proof to the IRS. It lives in Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2), and it matters because in an ordinary tax dispute you defend your own number. Under the safe harbor the government has to prove the valuation method or its application was grossly unreasonable, a far higher bar than simple disagreement.


### What are the three safe harbor methods under Treasury Reg 1.409A-1?


Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2) lists three qualifying methods: independent appraisal, formula price, and the illiquid start-up valuation by a qualified person. Those are subparagraphs (B)(2)(i), (B)(2)(ii), and (B)(2)(iii), and each carries its own conditions on dating, consistency, and company age. Subparagraph (B)(1) is the general reasonable-valuation rule that applies to everyone, not the safe harbor, and collapsing the two is the most common error in 409A content.


### Which safe harbor path do most growth-stage startups use?


Most growth-stage and venture-backed companies use path one, the independent appraisal under Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(i), dated within 12 months of the grant. Path one carries no company-age limit, no 90-day change-of-control test, and no 180-day offering test, since those gates belong to the illiquid start-up path instead. Indinero delivers path one appraisals inside a CFO advisory engagement, so the report holds up in a data room and feeds the ASC 718 current price input directly.


### What voids the safe harbor presumption?


A 409A loses safe harbor protection when it goes stale past 12 months, ignores new material information, or omits a factor the regulation requires. Material misstatement or omission to the appraiser voids it too, because that attacks the application of the method. With indinero the 409A sits with the team running your monthly close, so a converting bridge or a signed letter of intent surfaces before the next grant, not after it.


### Can the IRS still challenge a 409A under safe harbor?


Yes, the IRS can still challenge a 409A under safe harbor, but only by showing the valuation method or its application was grossly unreasonable. The safe harbor is a rebuttable presumption, not immunity. Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2) never defines grossly unreasonable, which in practice means a well-documented report with a defensible comparable set and a supported marketability discount is what stands between you and that argument.


### Is the illiquid startup formula method actually used in practice?


The formula price method is rarely used, because it requires a restriction on transfer that never lapses and consistent pricing for every insider transaction. That structure fits a company planning to stay closely held permanently, not one raising priced rounds toward an exit. The separate illiquid start-up method under Treasury Reg 1.409A-1(b)(5)(iv)(B)(2)(iii) does get used by young companies, though it closes once a business crosses ten years of operating history.


### What happens if the IRS rebuts the presumption of reasonableness?


A discounted option falls under Section 409A, so the holder owes income tax at vesting, a 20 percent additional tax, and premium interest. Income inclusion runs under IRC section 409A(a)(1)(A) as each tranche vests, not at exercise, so an employee who never exercised can still owe tax. The 20 percent sits in 409A(a)(1)(B)(i)(II), and California adds another 5 percent. The liability lands on the option holder while the company carries the Form W-2 reporting.
